en: The Philippine eagle, our national bird, uses its shaggy brown crest feathers to shield its eyes from heavy tropical rain.
Our national flower, the sampaguita, opens its white petals at night to release a strong fragrance that attracts pollinating moths.
The carabao, our national animal, wallows in deep mud to cool its body and protect its skin from biting insects.
The Ifugao people carved the Banaue Rice Terraces into mountains, using stone walls to hold water for irrigating their rice crops.
During the Lucban Pahiyas Festival, locals decorate houses with colorful kiping, which are leaf-shaped wafers made from ground rice.
Filipino scientist Ramon Barba invented a method using potassium nitrate to induce mango trees to flower and fruit year-round.
Mayon Volcano, a famous Philippine landmark, has a perfect cone shape formed by layers of cooled lava and volcanic ash.
The Philippine South Sea pearl, our national gem, forms inside the gold-lipped oyster found in the warm waters of Palawan.
The Tboli people of Mindanao weave the tnalak cloth by extracting and drying fibers from the abaca plant.
The Baguio Panagbenga Festival celebrates the blooming of local flowers in the Cordillera mountains after the cold December season.
Marine scientist Edgardo Gomez studied Philippine coral reefs, proving that healthy corals protect coastlines from strong ocean waves.
In Filipino folklore, the balete tree is considered a dwelling for spirits, recognizable by its long, hanging aerial roots.
